title: Fixture anchoring and load limits in walls
audience: Flat-pack and fixture installers who anchor shelves, cabinets, mirrors and wall-mounted items
learningOutcomes: Identify the load each fixture carries and the substrate that must carry it.
Choose anchors and fixings rated for the load and the wall type, using the manufacturer's data.
Refuse or refer a fixture whose load cannot be carried safely by the wall.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: NSW Government, Electricians: electrical licence for wiring work (last updated 1 December 2025); NSW Government, Plumbing, draining and gasfitting work (last updated 31 July 2026); Queensland Building and Construction Commission, When you need a licence (last published 18 August 2021; only part of this page has been confirmed); Energy Safe Victoria, Gasfitters (reviewed 31 May 2026). Electrical wiring work needs a licence whatever its price or kind.

instruction.heading: Work out the load before choosing an anchor
instruction.body: A wall-mounted fixture carries its own weight plus whatever is put on it, and the force on each fixing point is greater than the weight alone when the load sits at the end of a shelf or when someone pulls on the item. Work out the load from the item's specification, the contents it will hold and the way it will be used. Record the weight of the empty item, the weight of the expected contents, and the force at each fixing point, including the force from use. Use the worst-case load, not the average, because a shelf is often loaded unevenly and pulled from one end. Choose an anchor rated for that load. Manufacturers state a load rating for each anchor in each wall material, and that rating is the limit. A rating for a different wall material does not apply to the wall in front of you.

instruction.heading: Identify the substrate before drilling
instruction.body: Identify what the wall is made of before any fixing is chosen. Plasterboard is light and needs a fixing that spreads the load across the board, or a fixing into a stud or a noggin behind it. Masonry such as brick, concrete or block needs a masonry fixing of the right size and depth, and a drill and bit that suit the material. A hollow or cavity wall needs a fixing rated for a hollow substrate. Timber framing is a common target, but its position must be confirmed, not assumed. Use a stud finder and check the result by a second method where possible.

instruction.heading: Match the anchor to the wall and check for services
instruction.body: Once the substrate is known, choose a fixing that the manufacturer rates for that substrate and the calculated load. Where the load is heavy, fix into studs or solid substrate, with fixings that take the load into the structure. Do not rely on a plastic plug in plasterboard for a heavy load unless the manufacturer rates that plug for the load and the board. Before drilling, check for concealed cables and pipes, and stop if one is found or suspected. Concealed wiring is electrical work, and concealed pipes are plumbing or gas work, and both are licensed work in the states covered below. Refer the fixing to the licensed person, and do not drill into the service yourself to find out what it is. If the position of the fixing cannot be confirmed as clear of services, choose a different position or a different method, or refer the work.

instruction.heading: Install, test and record
instruction.body: Install the fixings to the manufacturer's directions, including the drill size, the depth and the torque or tightening method. After installation, test the fixing with a controlled load before the item is used. Do not use a fixing that moves, pulls out, cracks the surface or shows any sign of failure under the test. Record the item, the load, the substrate, the fixing used with its rating, the position of each fixing, the test result and the date. Where the wall cannot be confirmed as able to carry the load, do not hang the item on it. Refer the fixture or choose a different method, and record the referral and the reason.

instruction.heading: Dust, drilling and personal protection
instruction.body: Drilling into masonry or fibre-cement produces dust, and drilling into plasterboard produces fine material. Eye protection is needed whenever drilling. Hearing protection is needed where the noise cannot be eliminated. Dust controls and any respiratory protection depend on the site risk assessment. Do not assume that a dust mask is enough for masonry drilling without checking the risk assessment and the manufacturer's data for the mask.

procedure: Record the item's weight, the expected contents and the force at each fixing point, including the force from use.
Identify the wall type and locate studs, noggins or solid substrate, using a detector and a second check where possible.
Choose anchors and fixings rated for the calculated load and the substrate, and record the rating from the manufacturer's data.
Check for concealed cables, pipes and other services before drilling, and stop if one is found or suspected.
Install the fixings to the manufacturer's directions, using the drill size and depth the data gives.
Test each fixing with a controlled load before the item is used, using the manufacturer's test method where one is given.
Refer any fixture that cannot be confirmed as supported, and record the referral and the reason.

workedExamples.situation: A client wants a loaded bookshelf fixed to plasterboard with plastic wall plugs, and the bookshelf will hold heavy hardcover books.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the bookshelf be fixed with the plugs?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Heavy books on plasterboard need fixings rated for that load, and the plastic plugs supplied with the job are not shown to carry it without the manufacturer's rating for the board. Locate studs or noggins and fix into them, or use a fixing that the manufacturer rates for the load and the board. Record the rating and the calculated load. Refuse the plug method if the rating is not known, and record the refusal and the reason.

workedExamples.situation: Example only: a mirror is to be hung on a wall that the installer cannot identify. Behind the wall there may be a hollow cavity, and the position is near a power point.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the installer fix the mirror, and what must happen before drilling?
workedExamples.reasoning: Not yet. Move the fixing to a position where the substrate and the clearance from services can be confirmed, or refer the work to a licensed electrical worker before drilling. Once the substrate is known, choose a rated fixing for the mirror's weight and test it before the mirror is used. Stop, do not drill, and record the wall construction as unknown.

equipmentAndPpe: Fixings and anchors rated for the load and the wall, with the manufacturer's data on file
Drill and bits suited to the substrate, and eye protection
Hearing protection where noise cannot be eliminated
Test weights or a controlled test method, from the manufacturer's data, where the data specifies one

commonErrors.error: Using plastic plugs in plasterboard for heavy loads.
commonErrors.prevention: Fix into studs or noggins, or use fixings rated by the manufacturer for the load and the board.

commonErrors.error: Using the average load instead of the worst-case load at the end of a shelf.
commonErrors.prevention: Work out the load at each fixing point, including the force from use, and use the worst case.

commonErrors.error: Drilling without locating studs or services.
commonErrors.prevention: Locate studs and services first, and refer if the position cannot be confirmed as clear.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a fixing that held a light test will carry the full load.
commonErrors.prevention: Test with a controlled load, follow the manufacturer's method, and never use the fixing beyond its rating.

commonErrors.error: Treating a wall as plasterboard or solid without checking.
commonErrors.prevention: Where the wall type is not known, do not hang the item.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Where a fixing could reach a concealed electrical service, stop and refer the work to a licensed electrical worker. On the NSW Government page, electrical wiring work needs a licence whatever the job's price or kind, except for equipment operating at not more than 50 volts AC or 120 volts ripple-free DC. The page does not define wiring work in full. Check the issuer and class on the NSW licence pages before taking the work.

A concealed pipe found during fixing is plumbing or gas work and is referred to a licensed person. New South Wales: the licence or certificate covers plumbing, draining and gasfitting work whatever its price, and Building Commission NSW manages the licensing. Queensland: the QBCC page covers drainage, plumbing and gas fitting work at every value. The page was last published on 18 August 2021, so confirm the current rule with the QBCC. Victoria: Energy Safe Victoria's gasfitter page advises a licensed gasfitter for gas work, including renovations that disconnect or move gas appliances, and notes that the Victorian Building Authority administers gasfitter licensing.
Completing this lesson does not give an electrical, plumbing, gasfitting or building licence, and it does not authorise anchoring a fixture into a regulated service.

qualityStandard: The load at each fixing point is recorded before the fixings are chosen, including the force from use.
Each fixing is rated for the load and the substrate, with the rating recorded from the manufacturer's data.
Every fixing is checked for services before drilling, and the position is confirmed clear.
A fixture is not hung on a wall whose support cannot be confirmed.
documentationEvidence: Load and fixing record with the rating, the substrate and the position of each fixing
Test record for the installed fixture, with the test method and result
Referral note for any fixture or position not shown as supported or clear of services.
summary: Work out the load at each fixing point, including the force from use, before choosing an anchor.
Identify the substrate, then match the anchor to it, and fix into studs or solid substrate where the load requires it.
Check for concealed services before drilling, and refer any electrical, gas or plumbing work to the licensed person.
Refer any fixture that cannot be confirmed as supported, and record the referral.

knowledgeChecks.question: A loaded bookshelf is to be fixed to plasterboard with plastic plugs. What is correct?
options: Use the plugs because they are supplied with the job and the client has already paid for them
Use two plugs instead of four, since the shelf is light enough to hang on fewer fixings
Fix into studs or use a rated fixing, and refuse the plug method if the rating is not known
Hang it from the ceiling light, since the light fixing is strong enough to carry the load

knowledgeChecks.question: What should set the load for choosing an anchor?
options: The average expected load across the whole year of normal use
The weight of the empty item when it is delivered to the site
The client's preference for how the item should be fixed
The worst-case load at each fixing point, including force from use

knowledgeChecks.question: Before drilling a fixing position, what must be done?
options: Drill a test hole in the centre of the wall before any fixing is set
Identify the substrate, locate studs, and check for concealed services
Fix the item first and check the wall for services afterwards
Ask the client to confirm there are no pipes or cables in the wall
